questions.question: Three initiatives are on the table: improve activation, reduce large-workspace response time, and add meeting summaries. Each is described as a direction with no threshold. What is the practical consequence?
options: The team will pick the one with the clearest user demand
None of the three can lose the argument, so the choice is settled by who advocates hardest
The team will over-invest in whichever one is technically easiest to start
The team will need a scoring model to rank them
questions.explanation: A direction never completes, so it always deserves more effort and can never be outranked. Option D is the answer a PM gives after learning prioritization vocabulary — but scoring three directions just moves the same undefined comparison into a spreadsheet and gives it a number.

questions.question: Noted defines activation as creating a document and returning within seven days. What is the strongest objection to using this definition to judge the 11% decline?
options: Seven days is too short a window for a document tool
The definition has never been validated against a control group
Aggregate activation should always be segmented before it is used
It measures activity, and nothing establishes that the activity corresponds to the job the product does
questions.explanation: Noted's job is capture, direct, produce. Creating a document and returning can happen without a document ever becoming useful. Option C is tempting and true as far as it goes, but segmenting a definition that does not describe the job just gives you the same wrong measure split four ways.

questions.question: A PM writes: "Good means recovering 60% of the lost activation within one quarter." What is the most important thing still missing?
options: The population the threshold applies to, and what must not get worse for the recovery to count
A confidence interval on the 60% figure
The engineering estimate required to hit it
Agreement from the founder that 60% is the right target
questions.explanation: A threshold without a population lets a gain in one group hide a loss in another, and a threshold without floors lets the number be hit in a way that costs more than it earns. Option C is tempting because cost matters, but cost belongs in the trade-off, not in the definition of what good is.

questions.question: Noted is about to build its first AI-first onboarding. Nobody has watched a user go through it. What does defining good require here?
options: Set a threshold from the current activation baseline, then adjust it after launch
Skip the definition, since exploratory work is judged on learning rather than outcomes
Name the bar-setting moment: what you will observe, when, and what converts the observation into a threshold
Use the enterprise team lead population, because their behaviour is the most consequential
questions.explanation: This is the boundary. You cannot know the bar before you watch the behaviour, but "we'll know it when we see it" is not a definition. Option A is the disciplined-sounding trap: a number invented from an unrelated baseline gets defended later as if it had meant something.

questions.question: Two changes are proposed. One is a copy change on the empty document state, trivially reversible. One is a change to how documents are stored, costly to undo. A PM applies the same evidence bar to both. What is wrong?
options: Nothing — a consistent bar is what makes decisions comparable across the roadmap
The bar should follow reversibility, so the copy change is being over-built and the storage change under-built
The storage change should not be a product decision at all
The copy change needs a higher bar, because it touches the surface every new user sees
questions.explanation: How good is good enough depends on what it costs to be wrong and whether the correction is available. Option A is the trained answer — consistency sounds like rigor, but a uniform bar means you are simultaneously over-testing cheap reversible work and under-testing the work you cannot take back.
